content: Q fever is a zoonotic infection caused by Coxiella burnetii, which can present with a wide range of clinical manifestations involving multiple organ systems. It is classified into acute and chronic forms based on the duration and progression of symptoms. Acute Q Fever: 1. Flu-like Symptoms: The most common presentation includes an abrupt onset of high-grade fevers, often accompanied by chills and night sweats. Headaches are typically retrobulbar and may be associated with photophobia. Arthralgias (joint pain) are also frequently reported. 2. Pneumonia: Pneumonia in Q fever is usually mild and often discovered incidentally on chest X-rays. If a cough is present, it is typically dry and nonproductive. Other respiratory symptoms may include dyspnea (shortness of breath) and pleuritic chest pain. Rarely, the condition can progress to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), which is life-threatening. 3. Hepatitis: Patients may experience right upper quadrant abdominal pain, jaundice, and gastrointestinal symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and bloating. 4. Rare Acute Manifestations: Pericarditis and Myocarditis: These are uncommon but carry a poor prognosis. Symptoms include chest pain, dyspnea, and palpitations. Neurologic Findings: Meningoencephalitis may occur, presenting with headache, confusion, and seizures. Dermatologic Findings: Skin manifestations include maculopapular rash, diffuse punctate rash, and erythema nodosum. 5. Q Fever During Pregnancy: Most infections during pregnancy are asymptomatic, but complications can include intrauterine growth retardation (IUGR) and intrauterine fetal death (IUFD). Infections in the first trimester and placental involvement are associated with higher risks of fetal compromise. Chronic Q Fever: Chronic Q fever is a more severe and less common form of the disease, characterized by infection persisting for more than six months. It can develop years after an acute infection. 1. Endocarditis: This is the most common manifestation of chronic Q fever and is often culture-negative. Predisposing factors include valvular lesions, prosthetic valves, and immunocompromised states. Symptoms include low-grade fevers, palpitations, dyspnea, and embolic phenomena. 2. Skeletal Manifestations: Bone and joint infections are common in chronic Q fever, such as osteomyelitis or septic arthritis. 3. Cardiopulmonary Involvement: Chronic pleural or pericardial effusions and interstitial pulmonary fibrosis may present with dyspnea and fatigue. 4. Chronic Fatigue Syndrome: Up to 10% of patients with chronic Q fever may develop chronic fatigue syndrome. Physical Examination Findings: 1. Vital Signs: High-grade fevers with chills and night sweats. Tachycardia and tachypnea. 2. General Appearance: Patients often appear acutely ill. 3. Skin: Maculopapular or punctate rash, erythema nodosum, and spider nevi (in cases of hepatic decompensation). 4. HEENT: Jaundice may be present. Congested neck veins in cases of heart failure due to endocarditis or myocarditis. 5. Lungs: Minimal auscultatory findings in most cases. Crackles, especially in the lower lung fields, or decreased breath sounds if pleural effusion is present. 6. Abdomen: Hepatomegaly and ascites in cases of chronic hepatitis. 7. Heart: An S3 gallop due to hyperdynamic circulation. New-onset murmurs in endocarditis. Pericardial rub and distant heart sounds in pericarditis or pericardial effusion. 8. Neurological Examination: Neck rigidity and positive Brudzinski and Kernig signs in meningoencephalitis. Signs of increased intracranial pressure, such as vomiting, convulsions, and papilledema. 9. Extremities: Tenderness over affected joints and bones. Lower limb edema in the presence of heart failure. Pathogenesis: 1. Transmission: The primary mode of transmission is inhalation of contaminated aerosols. Other routes include ingestion of raw dairy products, vertical transmission (mother to fetus), and tick bites. 2. Bacterial Forms: Coxiella burnetii exists in two forms: Small cell form: Resistant to environmental stressors like heat, pressure, and disinfectants. Large cell form: The metabolically active form that persists in macrophages within acidic vacuoles. 3. Antigenic Phases: Phase I: Smooth lipopolysaccharide capsule, associated with acute infection. Phase II: Rough lipopolysaccharide capsule, associated with chronic infection. Diagnostic Testing: 1. Serologic Testing: Indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) is the preferred method for antibody detection. Antibodies to phase II antigens are tested first, followed by phase I if positive. Serologic follow-up is recommended every three months for two years after acute infection to monitor for chronic Q fever. 2. Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR): PCR can detect C. burnetii DNA in clinical samples and is particularly useful in early infection or seronegative cases. 3. Cultures: C. burnetii does not grow on standard blood cultures but can be cultivated in specialized media, such as embryonated eggs or cell cultures. 4. Liver Function Tests: Elevated AST and ALT levels (2-3 times the normal range) are common. 5. Imaging: Chest X-rays may show atypical pneumonia or interstitial fibrosis in chronic cases. CT scans can reveal scattered opacities or lobar consolidation. Q Fever as a Biological Weapon: Coxiella burnetii is highly virulent and has been considered a potential biological weapon. According to WHO estimates, dispersing 50 kg of C. burnetii over a 2 km² area could infect 500,000 individuals, causing acute illness in 125,000 and chronic illness in 9,000, with 150 fatalities. Microscopic Pathology: Coxiella burnetii is a gram-negative, polymorphic intracellular organism. It was previously classified as a rickettsia but is now considered a proteobacterium. Differential Diagnosis: Q fever must be differentiated from other diseases causing gram-negative endocarditis, such as HACEK endocarditis, and from other atypical pneumonias like Mycoplasma, Legionella, and Chlamydia pneumonia.
